item.title: The heron and the hawk
item.description:
One year around the turn of the millennium, me and my girlfriend at the time, Angelica, decided to spend an Easter vacation in Aegina, a beautiful and serene little island just south of Athens. During that period Angelica was volunteering for the Greek Center for the Protection of Wild Animals (Ελληνικό Κέντρο Περίθαλψης Αγρίων Ζώων / ΕΚΠΑΖ / EKPAZ) in Athens, and for several years already we had both been volunteers at Greenpeace Greece. As such, we were both in a sense insiders of the relatively small environmental movement of Greece. So, we were told that while we were in Aegina we could visit the new EKPAZ facilities on the island. We were told that they would be closed to the public due to Easter, but we could go, and the personnel would be there, and they would be happy to see us.
The EKPAZ logo; photo from ekpaz.com

In previous years, EKPAZ had been housed in a very old building complex in the town of Aegina. Built in 1828, it was originally an orphanage, then used for various purposes such as military academy, psychiatric hospital, quarantine station, refugee asylum, etc. but for most of its existence, that is from 1880 until 1985, it was a jailhouse. (Little known fact: for most of that time, it was primarily receiving political prisoners.) After it was shut down in 1985 it fell into disuse. In 1990 it was granted to EKPAZ for use as an animal hospital.

I have heard that the conditions in it were not particularly nice, and this was probably putting it mildly.
Aerial view of the old jailhouse of Aegina; photo from lifo.gr
Street view of the old jailhouse of Aegina; photo from lalaounistravel.com
Inside view of the old orphanage / jailhouse of Aegina during the EKPAZ years; photo from ethnos.gr

In 2001 the municipality started making plans to turn the old jailhouse into a museum, so they had EKPAZ relocate. This time they granted them a recently constructed hill-side building complex in a slightly remote inland location of Aegina. It was originally intended as a cultural center, but it had never materialized as such.
The new facilities of EKPAZ (zoom out); photo from ekpaz.com
The new facilities of EKPAZ (zoom in); photo from ekpaz.com

I cannot say that I know for sure how and why this cultural center that nobody needed had popped up in the middle of nowhere, but it seemed to me like one more of those projects that are unfortunately common in Greece, where European Union funds are secured for projects that have no purpose other than to appropriate such funds. The standard play is that a proposal is submitted for public a work for which the EU will provide 50% funding; the work is completed for only 10% of the cost, another 20% or so goes to pay taxes, (because invoices are issued for 100% of the cost, to justify the 50% funding,) and the remaining 20% or so, often amounting to hundreds of thousands of Euros, goes into the pockets of those involved in the fraud. The end-result is invariably useless. In this particular case, the location was too remote to be practical, and keeping the facilities running would have required a regular flow of money that there was no budget for; so, since the municipality had no use for the facilities, they let EKPAZ have them. One thing is sure: for EKPAZ, the modern housing constituted a huge improvement over the old jailhouse.

And so on Easter Sunday of 2002 we went there. We were greeted by a handful of friendly faces; some were employees, I think most were volunteers. They had all gathered there on that day for a certain Easter Sunday tradition that is very strong in Greece: the roasting of the lamb.

This is one of the many paradoxes of the environmental movement in Greece: in any other country of the Western World, a large percentage of the people involved with environmentalism, and especially people involved with the protection of animals, would be vegetarian if not vegan. This would prevent the slightest notion of any kind of roasting of any kind of animal; but this is not so in Greece, which has a virtually non-existent vegetarian culture. As a result, it is perfectly possible in Greece to see people attending to injured wild animals, while at the same time, a little bit further away, the same people are roasting an animal that had the misfortune of being neither wild, nor injured.

This is not to say that either me or Angelica were vegetarians; from a dietary perspective, we were omnivorous just like the rest; however, we could not indicate any great interest in standing around the roasting of the lamb, because it is, quite frankly, a ghastly sight to behold. So, it was agreed that one of the volunteers would give us a tour of the facilities.

Being admitted in the place, despite it being closed to the public on that day, and then having a tour guide all for ourselves, made us feel like we were guests of honor. We were very grateful for that.

First we visited the veterinarian's cabin. Is was a tiny house which may have consisted of just one room. (And maybe a bathroom?) It was equipped with an examination table, various diagnostic equipment, and other medical supplies. I do not know much about medical stuff, but my impression was that it was decently equipped and well kept. The lady working there was Maria Ganoti, a well-known figure in environmental circles in Greece.

I suppose that when you are in this kind of job you don't take a day off, because you know that the injured animals will not stop arriving just because it is your day off.

Sure enough, we had hardly introduced ourselves when I saw through the window a motorcycle arriving outside and parking in a hurry. It was a BMW GS 1000, as huge and formidable as expensive. The rider, dressed in impeccable (and also quite expensive) motorcycle gear got off the saddle, picked up a box from the luggage compartment, and rushed into the clinic.

He was a very tall and very handsome young man. His long hair and unshaved look did not manage to make him look particularly rough; you could tell he was a rich kid living a good life. I thought that he might be some kind of celebrity who chooses to invest his free time in activities with a noble cause instead of whatever it is that celebrities otherwise do with their free time. In poor countries like Greece where disposable income is rare, people tend to have more pressing needs to attend to than the environment or the well-being of animals; thus, the affluent tend to be over-represented within the tiny environmental movement.

Heck, come to think of it, even I can be considered as an example of this phenomenon: oh look, what a coincidence, I was also there on a BMW motorcycle, albeit one of about half the size, and less than half the price, but nonetheless a symbol of almost certainly making ends meet. I had to acknowledge that my comparatively decent salary of a Software Engineer gave me the luxury of not worrying about the rent at the end of each month. Quite often we are not aware of privileges we enjoy.

The motorcycle man raised his arms with great purpose to hand the box to Maria. She took it, and he lowered his arms as someone whose mission had been accomplished. He stayed to see what was going to happen with the content of the box. We were all curious to see what was in it.

Maria opened the box, reached inside, and took out one of the most beautiful creatures I have seen in my life. It was a little falcon. His plumage was not particularly fancy, just shades of grey, (so, probably male,) but around his eyes and at the base of the beak he had these incredibly bright orange pigments that made him look completely out of this world. (Either that, or, I thought, I do not really know much about this world.) According to research I did for the purposes of this post more than two decades later, he must have been a Red-footed falcon (falco vespertinus). The Greek name appears to be Μαυροκιρκίνεζο. The photo that I have found barely does any justice to what my eyes saw back then: this photo is very nice; what I saw was incredible.
Red-footed falcon (falco vespertinus) photo by Michele Mendi, from lipu.it

Maria held the little falcon in her hands and carefully felt every millimeter of it with her fingers. After a few moments she had found what was wrong with the little fella: he had a broken wing. She started to apply a bandage that would immobilize it and let it heal, and she did it with such dexterity that it was obvious that she had done the same thing uncountable times before. We were very lucky to be given the opportunity to witness this incident and to see her at work.

We proceeded to a building where many injured wild birds were kept. I remember storks, cranes, flamingos, swans, herons, pelicans, and other kinds of birds that I don't know their names. They all seemed pretty miserable. Our guide assured us that they were all going to make it, they just had to stay in the facility for a while to recuperate. She said that all these birds were there because they had been injured by birdshot, despite all of them belonging to species that are never legal to hunt.

This is the sad reality of "sport" hunting in Greece: laws and regulations exist like in any other civilized country, but people treat them as mostly decorative, and the state lacks the resources necessary to enforce them. The last time that a Greek chose to die in order to abide by the laws was two and a half thousand years ago.

Keeping such a large number of birds in an enclosed space had a very unfortunate consequence: the room stank with not just the worst stench that I have ever experienced in my life, but I would dare say, a stench that was worse than any stench imaginable. Our guide did not seem to have much of an issue with it; I suppose it is something that you get used to after a while; but while I stood there, I started feeling like I was under physical assault. When we exited the building I was very glad to be able to breathe again.

Then we walked down a paved path towards a little house that stood aside from the rest of the buildings. The path had a beautiful view through an opening between two hills, through which one could see some more of the hills of Aegina, and then out in the distance what I suppose must have been a Peloponesian mountain range, and then out in the extreme distance yet one more Peloponesian mountain range. For the needs of this post I managed to find a photo showing that exact same view.
Paved path with a view, leading to small house; photo from ekpaz.com

The path led us in front of the outdoor cages, which were for animals that were doing a bit better than the ones in the enclosed building. We saw a few animals that were not birds, for example a wild boar. I was glad to see that the cages for the large birds were spacious, allowing them some freedom of movement. Especially the one for the vultures was huge. We stopped in front of it to look at the vultures. I had never seen one before.

Vultures seem to be over-represented at EKPAZ, probably because people hate them. I suppose that "sport" hunters who would have it at nothing to shoot a stork might even go out of their way to shoot a vulture. Of course arbitrary human prejudice reigns supreme over naturalist nonsense like compassionate conservation, respect for all of nature, etc.

I could not help but briefly recall the numbers:

  • One in every five birds that are hit by birdshot are never retrieved by the hunters who shot them.
  • Of those, many die instantly but fell into dense cover, while others escape with injuries.
  • Of those that escape with injuries, the vast majority die of those injuries soon afterwards, and only a tiny percentage survives.
  • A much smaller percentage is found by humans who have nothing to do with hunting.
  • Of those, only an exceedingly small percentage is lucky enough to be found by humans who will go out of their way to inquire what one is supposed to do when one finds an injured wild animal, will find out that one is supposed to contact EKPAZ, will diligently do so, and after receiving instructions on how to ship the animal to EKPAZ, will again diligently do so.
  • Those exceedingly few birds that have the incredible luck to arrive at EKPAZ still alive were the ones that I was looking at in the cages in front of me.

So, for every single bird in these cages there were perhaps a thousand other birds that had died of their injuries, and five times that many more that had been shot dead.

All of them belonging to species under protection, and therefore illegal to hunt.

What the fuck is wrong with humans?

We started walking along the last segment of the path, towards the little house at the end of it.

Already from a distance I had noticed something strange: in front of the little house were two birds; one stocky and brownish, the other slender and white. They were just standing there, motionless, a couple of meters from each other, doing nothing in particular. First I thought that they must be in cages, perhaps made of very thin wire and therefore invisible from a distance, but I soon realized that no such thing was happening: the birds were indeed standing in the open. I found that very odd. I would have expected those birds to either be in cages, or to have flown away.

As we drew closer, I could tell that the brown one was a hawk, and the white one was a heron, and each of them looked quite all right: it was not like they were missing plumage or body parts. How could these two birds, belonging to very different species, be simply standing there, in the open, at such close proximity to each other? This was certainly not the natural habitat of the heron, who belongs to rivers, lakes, and sweet-water wetlands, and it probably was not the natural habitat of the hawk either, because I they belong to the woodlands of mainland Greece, not the barren islands of the Aegean sea. So, what were those two doing there?

Seeing that they were standing motionless, I seriously pondered for a moment that they might be embalmed,. Of course it was preposterous to think that EKPAZ would have placed two embalmed birds there, but not as preposterous as to suggest that these two birds would have chosen by themselves to go stand there. However, I soon noticed a tiny bit of movement, so the embalmment theory was disproven, and I was back at simply finding this a very highly unlikely sight to behold and not knowing what to make out of it.

The puzzlement became only greater as we approached, and the birds did not fly or even walk away. However, I took some comfort in noticing that our guide was approaching the birds without showing any signs of surprise, so I figured that this is normal, and it somehow ends up having a logical explanation, which was about to be revealed.

We were now standing among the birds. Both of them looked healthy and beautiful. Their shiny eyes, those marvels of nature that give them a 360 degree view of the world with a level of detail that humans could never imagine, were paying no particular attention to us, as we were practically towering above them.

For the purposes of this post I found photos of two birds that look exactly like those two at EKPAZ.
A white heron (little egret) (Wikipedia); Image credit: wikipedia.org
A hawk (long-legged buzzard) (Wikipedia); Image credit: wikipedia.org

Our guide went inside the little house and came out holding a bag of some kind of birdfeed. She poured some of it into a container on the ground nearby, producing the distinctive sound of dozens of little pellets hitting metal. The heron walked over to it and started eating.

Then she went back inside, and came out holding a piece of raw meat. First she placed the meat on a rock that had probably been there for that purpose, and then she lifted the hawk with her bare hands, (the hawk incredibly not minding at all,) and placed it on the rock, right on top of the meat. The hawk felt the meat with its feet, and then started ripping the meat with its claws and eating it.

Finally, she explained:

She said that both those birds were blind. She said that they looked perfectly well, but the optic nerves of each bird had been destroyed by birdshot. Then she said something that struck me as both an interesting fact that was completely new to me, and at the same time as a self-evident truth that I should have been able to guess by myself:

A blind bird will not fly.

So, unlike most other birds, these two were going to stay with EKPAZ forever.

I turned my face towards the lady as to keep my welling eyes entirely behind the sunglasses, but to no avail, as gravity dragged the teardrops down my face.

We moved on.

The friendly people of EKPAZ invited us to stay and have lunch with them, but added that we would have to wait some more, because the lamb had taken a lot longer than they had expected to properly roast. So, it was not ready yet, despite it being something like 3 o'clock in the afternoon. To their credit, they were inexperienced in this; who knows, perhaps none of them had roasted a lamb before. We thanked them, but decided to return to the town, not because we were vegetarians, but due to a combination of other factors, having to do with the whole experience of visiting the facilities being slightly overwhelming, and neither of us particularly caring for lamb, or for traditions. But we were both very thankful for having been invited and given the tour.
